question.title: RBAC Scope Selection
question.scenario: You must allow a support team to restart VMs and read VM metrics, but only in the Prod-App1 resource group. They must not manage networking or IAM anywhere else.
question.question-text: Where and how should you assign permissions?

choices.choice: Assign an Azure RBAC role at the Prod-App1 resource group scope
Assign the Contributor role at the subscription level
Assign the Global Administrator role at the tenant level
Create a custom role with permissions on all resource groups

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about where in the Azure hierarchy you should scope permissions to limit the blast radius to exactly one resource group.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Assigning an Azure RBAC role at the Prod-App1 resource group scope (A) is correct because it constrains permissions to only that RG. Option B (Contributor at subscription) grants far too much access across all resource groups, violating least privilege. Option C (Global Administrator) is a tenant-level Entra ID role that has nothing to do with scoped Azure resource management. Option D (custom role on all RGs) defeats the purpose of restricting to a single resource group. Always assign at the narrowest scope that satisfies the requirement, and prefer built-in roles like Virtual Machine Contributor over broad roles like Contributor.

ul.li: RBAC scope inheritance flows downward: management group to subscription to resource group to resource. Assigning at subscription leaks privileges to every RG, so always target the narrowest scope that meets the need.
The built-in Virtual Machine Contributor role covers VM restart and management but not networking or IAM. Pair it with Monitoring Reader if the team also needs metric access from Azure Monitor.
Best practice is to assign roles to an Entra ID security group rather than individual users. This simplifies onboarding, offboarding, and audit reviews.
If metric data is stored in a separate Log Analytics workspace, the team may also need Log Analytics Reader on that workspace, since workspace permissions are independent of resource-level RBAC.

question.title: Policy: Enforce Tags
question.scenario: Finance requires every resource to have tags: CostCenter, Owner, Env. Noncompliant deployments must fail in prod, but only be reported in dev.

choices.choice: Azure Policy with deny effect in prod and audit effect in dev
RBAC roles that prevent resource creation without tags
Resource locks on all resources without tags
Azure Blueprints with automatic tag assignment

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The requirement has two environments with different enforcement levels. Which Azure governance tool supports per-scope effect tuning?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Azure Policy with deny in prod and audit in dev (A) is correct. You create a policy initiative requiring CostCenter, Owner, and Env tags, then assign it with the deny effect to prod subscriptions (blocking noncompliant deployments) and with the audit effect to dev subscriptions (reporting only). Option B is wrong because RBAC controls actions on resources, not their configuration properties like tags. Option C is wrong because resource locks prevent deletion or modification of existing resources, not tag enforcement at creation. Option D is partially relevant but Blueprints do not dynamically enforce tag presence on every deployment the way Policy does.

ul.li: The built-in policy definition "Require a tag and its value on resources" uses the deny effect. For multiple tags, group several such definitions into a custom initiative and assign once per scope.
The modify effect can auto-apply tags inherited from the resource group, but not all resource types support modify. Always test auto-tagging against target resource providers before relying on it.
Policy deny failures surface as ARM deployment errors with a policy compliance error code. Teams must understand that a "deployment failed" error may be policy-driven, not an infrastructure problem.
Use policy exemptions sparingly. Every exemption should have a documented business justification and ideally an expiration date to prevent permanent compliance gaps.

question.title: VM Extension for Configuration
question.scenario: You must run a one-time bootstrap script on 100 VMs after deployment.

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: You need to run a script on 100 VMs without logging in to each one. What Azure VM capability supports remote, automated script execution?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: The Custom Script Extension (A) is correct because it downloads and executes scripts on Azure VMs automatically, making it ideal for post-deployment bootstrapping at scale. Option B (manually RDP) is impractical for 100 VMs and does not scale. Option C (Azure Bastion) provides secure remote access but does not automate script execution. Option D (Azure Monitor) is for monitoring and alerting, not configuration management. For VMSS, the Custom Script Extension is added to the scale set model so every new instance automatically runs the bootstrap script on creation.

ul.li: Custom Script Extension scripts must be idempotent because the extension agent may retry execution on transient failures. Write scripts so re-running them does not cause errors or duplicate work (e.g., check if software is already installed before installing again).

Scripts are typically stored in Azure Blob Storage with a SAS URL or in a public GitHub repository. For production, use a private blob container with a time-limited SAS token to avoid exposing scripts publicly.

The extension has a default timeout of 90 minutes for execution. Long-running installations should either be broken into phases or use Run Command for ad-hoc execution instead of relying on the extension timeout.

Alternatives for more complex configuration management include Azure Desired State Configuration (DSC) extension, cloud-init for Linux VMs, and Azure Automanage. Choose based on whether you need one-time setup versus ongoing configuration enforcement.

question.title: Network Segmentation with Subnets
question.scenario: You have a VNet with web, app, data tiers. You need to restrict web -> data directly but allow web -> app -> data.

choices.choice: NSGs applied to subnets with explicit allow/deny rules for required flows
Use a single NSG for all subnets

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: You need different allow/deny rules on each subnet. What is the lightest-weight Azure tool for per-subnet traffic filtering?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: NSGs applied to subnets with explicit allow/deny rules (A) is correct because each tier gets its own NSG with rules that allow only the intended traffic flows: web to app on specific ports, app to data on specific ports, and an explicit deny from web to data. Option B (Azure Firewall) works but is more complex and costly for simple inter-subnet filtering. Option C (route tables without NSGs) controls traffic path but not access control. Option D (single NSG for all subnets) cannot differentiate rules per subnet since the same rules would apply everywhere. Per-subnet NSGs are the standard pattern for micro-segmentation within a VNet.

ul.li: NSG rules are evaluated by priority number (lowest number = highest priority), and the first matching rule wins. Default rules allow all intra-VNet traffic, so you must add explicit deny rules to block web-to-data communication before the default allow-VNet rule matches.

Application Security Groups (ASGs) let you group VMs logically (e.g., WebServers, AppServers, DataServers) and reference those groups in NSG rules instead of IP addresses. This eliminates IP-based rule sprawl and makes rules self-documenting.

NSGs can be applied at both the subnet level and the NIC level. When both are present, inbound traffic must pass the subnet NSG first, then the NIC NSG. For simplicity, most designs use subnet-level NSGs only and reserve NIC-level NSGs for exceptional cases.

NSG flow logs record allowed and denied traffic and can be sent to a Log Analytics workspace for analysis. Enable flow logs on each NSG to verify that your segmentation rules are working as intended and to detect unexpected traffic patterns.

question.title: Monitoring: Metrics vs Logs
question.scenario: You need near-real-time alerting when VM CPU > 90% for 10 minutes.
question.question-text: Should you use logs or metrics?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The alert must be near-real-time and based on a simple numeric threshold. Which Azure Monitor signal type has the lowest evaluation latency?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: A metrics alert (D) is the correct choice because Azure Monitor metrics are collected at one-minute granularity by default and metric alert rules evaluate with near-real-time latency (typically under one minute). Option A (log-based alerts with KQL) can work but has higher evaluation latency (minimum 5 minutes for log queries) and is overkill for a simple CPU threshold. Option B (Azure Advisor) provides optimization recommendations, not real-time alerts. Option C (Activity Log alerts) detects control-plane operations like resource creation or deletion, not data-plane metrics like CPU utilization. Metrics alerts are purpose-built for numeric threshold monitoring with configurable aggregation windows.

ul.li: When configuring a metric alert for CPU, choose the aggregation type carefully. Average CPU over 10 minutes catches sustained high load, while Maximum catches brief spikes. For the "greater than 90% for 10 minutes" scenario, use Average aggregation with a 10-minute window.

Metric alerts support dynamic thresholds that use machine learning to establish baselines and detect anomalies. This is useful when a fixed 90% threshold does not account for normal workload patterns that vary by time of day.

Metrics are retained for 93 days at progressively coarser granularity: 1-minute for 30 days, 5-minute for 60 days, then hourly. For longer retention or complex queries, send metrics to a Log Analytics workspace using diagnostic settings.

Log-based alerts shine for complex conditions that involve joining multiple tables (e.g., correlate high CPU with specific error messages in application logs). For simple threshold monitoring, metrics alerts are always the faster and cheaper option.

question.title: Alert Noise Control
question.scenario: Your alert triggers every minute and spams on-call during sustained high CPU.
question.question-text: What change reduces noise while staying responsive?

choices.choice: Use stateful alerting and adjust frequency/suppression

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The problem is repeated notifications for the same ongoing condition. What alerting behavior fires once on entry and once on exit instead of every cycle?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Using stateful alerting and adjusting frequency/suppression (B) is correct. Stateful metric alerts fire once when the condition is first met and automatically resolve when the condition clears, preventing repeated notifications during sustained high CPU. You can also tune the evaluation frequency (e.g., every 5 minutes instead of every minute) and set action rule suppression windows. Option A (disable) eliminates monitoring entirely. Option C (threshold 100%) means the alert practically never fires, which is not responsive. Option D (remove action group) keeps the alert but removes all notifications, making it useless. Well-tuned stateful alerts balance responsiveness with noise reduction.

ul.li: Azure Monitor metric alerts are stateful by default since 2019. Each alert fires (Activated), stays active while the condition persists, and resolves (Deactivated) when the condition clears. Verify your alert rules are not configured as stateless, which causes repeated firing.

Action rules (formerly alert processing rules) can suppress notifications during planned maintenance windows or apply time-based filtering. For example, suppress non-critical alerts between 2 AM and 4 AM during a scheduled patch window.

Alert fatigue is a leading cause of operational failures. Teams that receive too many alerts start ignoring them. Review alert firing frequency monthly and tune thresholds, aggregations, and evaluation windows to keep the signal-to-noise ratio high.

For complex alerting scenarios, use action groups with multiple notification channels (email for awareness, SMS for urgency, webhook for automation). Route critical alerts to PagerDuty or ServiceNow via webhook for proper incident management with escalation policies.

question.title: Key Vault Integration for Secrets
question.scenario: Apps running on VMs need to retrieve secrets without storing credentials on disk.

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The goal is zero credentials on disk. What Azure identity feature lets a VM prove who it is to other services without storing any secret?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Managed identity plus Key Vault access (B) is the preferred pattern because the VM gets an automatically managed identity from Azure that can authenticate to Key Vault without any credentials stored on disk or in code. Option A (environment variables) still stores secrets in cleartext on the VM. Option C (embed in code) is the worst practice since secrets end up in source control. Option D (storage account keys) does not address the general secret management problem and still requires storing the keys somewhere. With managed identity, the app calls the local Instance Metadata Service to get a token, then uses that token to retrieve secrets from Key Vault at runtime, creating a zero-credential-on-disk architecture.

ul.li: System-assigned managed identity is tied to the VM lifecycle (deleted when the VM is deleted) and is simpler for single-resource scenarios. User-assigned managed identity can be shared across multiple VMs and survives VM deletion, making it better for scale sets and reusable configurations.

Having a managed identity does not automatically grant Key Vault access. You must explicitly assign a Key Vault access role (e.g., Key Vault Secrets User for RBAC model) or create an access policy entry (for the access policy model) for the managed identity principal ID.

If the Key Vault has network restrictions (private endpoint or firewall), ensure the VM can reach the Key Vault endpoint. A private endpoint on Key Vault requires the correct private DNS zone linked to the VM's VNet, or the managed identity token exchange will succeed but the Key Vault API call will fail with a network error.

Key Vault supports two permission models: vault access policies (legacy) and Azure RBAC (recommended). RBAC provides finer-grained control, supports Entra ID Conditional Access, and integrates with Azure PIM for just-in-time access. New deployments should use RBAC.

question.title: VM Patch Management Concept
question.scenario: You need a consistent patching approach across many VMs with reporting.
question.question-text: What Azure-native option is commonly used?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The scenario needs scheduled patching with compliance reporting across many VMs. Is this a manual task or does Azure have a native service for it?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Azure Update Management or Update Manager (A) is correct because it provides a centralized, Azure-native solution for scheduling patches, reporting compliance status, and managing update rings across fleets of Windows and Linux VMs. Option B (manual patching) does not scale beyond a handful of VMs and provides no compliance reporting. Option C (reinstalling VMs monthly) is extremely disruptive and impractical for stateful workloads. Option D (marketplace images only) provides a patched base image but does not address ongoing patch management after deployment. Azure Update Manager integrates with Azure Policy for compliance assessment and supports maintenance windows to control when patches are applied.

ul.li: Azure Update Manager (the current service name) has replaced the older Automation-based Update Management. It works without an Automation Account or Log Analytics workspace dependency, using the Azure VM agent directly. Verify the current service name and feature set, as Microsoft evolves this tooling frequently.

Maintenance configurations let you define recurring schedules (e.g., second Saturday at 2 AM) and associate them with VMs or dynamic scopes. Critical security patches can be set to auto-install outside the maintenance window for zero-day response.

For Windows VMs, the Azure VM agent orchestrates with Windows Update. For Linux VMs, it integrates with the native package manager (apt, yum, zypper). Prerequisites include the Azure VM agent being healthy and outbound connectivity to update sources.

Coordinate patching with application availability. Use Azure Update Manager's pre and post scripts to drain load balancer connections before patching and re-enable them after, ensuring zero-downtime updates for multi-instance workloads.

question.title: Restore vs Recreate (Disaster Recovery Thinking)
question.scenario: A VM is corrupted after a bad change. You have backups.
question.question-text: What's the fastest likely recovery path?

choices.choice: Restore from backup (or restore disks) and redeploy
Wait for the VM to self-heal

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: When a VM is corrupted and you have recent backups, the fastest path is to restore to a known good state rather than rebuilding from scratch or waiting.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Restoring from backup or restoring disks and redeploying (C) is the fastest recovery path because Azure Backup maintains application-consistent snapshots that can be restored to a known good point-in-time. You can either restore the full VM (creates a new VM from the backup) or restore just the disks and attach them to an existing or new VM. Option A (rebuild from scratch) requires reinstalling the OS, applications, and data, which takes significantly longer. Option B (Azure Support) adds wait time and is appropriate for platform issues, not customer-caused corruption. Option D (self-heal) is not how Azure VMs work when the OS or application is corrupted. The backup restore preserves all data and configuration up to the backup point.

ul.li: Azure Backup offers multiple restore options: Create New VM (provisions a new VM from backup), Restore Disks (restores managed disks to a storage account or resource group for manual attachment), and Replace Existing (swaps the current VM disks with backup versions). Choose based on whether you need the original VM identity, IP, and configuration preserved.

If a security incident is suspected (malware, ransomware), restore into an isolated quarantine VNet first. Do not restore to the production network until the backup has been scanned and validated. This prevents re-infection from a compromised backup.

Restore time depends on the backup tier. Instant restore from the snapshot tier (retained 1-5 days) takes minutes because the data is already in managed disk snapshots. Vault-tier restores require data transfer from the vault and can take hours depending on VM size and disk count.

For critical workloads, test restore procedures regularly. A backup that has never been test-restored is an assumption, not a guarantee. Document the restore runbook including network configuration, DNS updates, and application startup verification steps.

question.title: Log Analytics Workspace Access
question.scenario: A user can view VM resources but cannot query logs in Log Analytics.
question.question-text: Why, and what do you change?

choices.choice: Workspace permissions are separate; grant workspace access
The user needs Global Administrator role

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The user can see VMs but cannot query their logs. Are resource permissions and log query permissions governed by the same RBAC assignment?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Workspace permissions are separate and must be explicitly granted (A). A user with Reader on a VM can see the VM resource in the portal but cannot query its logs in Log Analytics because the workspace has its own RBAC model. You need to assign a workspace-level role like Log Analytics Reader or Monitoring Reader on the Log Analytics workspace itself. Option B (Global Administrator) is massively over-privileged for reading logs. Option C is incorrect because Azure Monitor cannot be globally disabled. Option D is unlikely since the scenario implies logs exist but are inaccessible. The separation of resource RBAC and workspace RBAC is a common source of confusion for teams new to Azure monitoring.

ul.li: Log Analytics supports two access control modes: workspace-context (permissions on the workspace grant access to all data in it) and resource-context (permissions on a resource grant access to that resource's logs in any workspace). The access mode is set on the workspace and affects how authorization is evaluated.

In resource-context mode, a user with Reader on a VM can query that VM's logs even without explicit workspace permissions. This is useful for large organizations where workspace admins should not have to manage per-user access. Check the workspace Access Control Mode setting in Properties.

Central Log Analytics workspaces often reside in a shared platform subscription, separate from the application subscriptions. Users need permissions at the workspace scope, which is in a different subscription than their application resources. Cross-subscription RBAC assignment is required.

For fine-grained access, use table-level RBAC to restrict users to specific log tables within the workspace (e.g., allow access to SecurityEvent but not ContainerLog). This is useful for compliance scenarios where different teams should only see specific data categories.

question.title: Resource Move: RG vs Subscription
question.scenario: You must move a set of resources to a new subscription for billing separation.
question.question-text: What are the two key prechecks?

choices.choice: Check if resources are running and stop them
Delete the resources and recreate them
Validate move support and ensure dependencies/permissions across scopes

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Not all resource types can be moved, and a cross-subscription move spans two security boundaries. What two things must you verify before attempting it?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Validating move support and ensuring dependencies/permissions across scopes (C) is correct. The two critical prechecks are: (1) confirm each resource type supports cross-subscription move using the Azure documentation move support matrix, since some resources cannot be moved at all; (2) verify you have required permissions in both the source and destination subscriptions (typically Contributor on both, plus specific permissions for resource types that require them). Option A (stop resources) is unnecessary for most resource moves. Option B (delete and recreate) loses resource IDs, configurations, and data. Option D (contact Support) is unnecessary for standard moves. Additionally, use the Move Validation API to pre-check before executing the actual move.

ul.li: Resource move support varies significantly by resource type. VMs, storage accounts, and VNets generally support cross-subscription moves, but some resources (classic resources, certain marketplace offerings) do not. Always check the official "Move operation support for resources" documentation before planning a move.

Dependent resources must be moved together or decoupled first. For example, a VM with managed disks, NICs, and a public IP must have all these resources moved in the same operation. If any dependency cannot be moved, the entire move fails validation.

RBAC role assignments are not moved with resources. After moving resources to a new subscription, re-create any role assignments that were specific to the old subscription scope. Managed identity associations may also need to be re-validated.

Azure Policy in the destination subscription can reject moved resources if they violate compliance rules (e.g., wrong tags, disallowed SKUs, missing configurations). Pre-check the destination subscription policies and remediate any expected compliance gaps before initiating the move.
